title: How To Hold Difficult Students Accountable
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Prompted by a reader question, Linsin restates his core position that difficult students should be held accountable exactly like everyone else — a calm, brief delivery of the consequence followed by walking away, which prompts self-reflection rather than defensiveness. He then addresses a nuance the reader raised: what to do when a teacher has built real rapport with a formerly difficult student and worries that enforcing a consequence might damage that fragile, developing relationship. Linsin's answer is a small but meaningful adjustment in phrasing — acknowledging the student's recent improvement before delivering the consequence, using language like "I have to give you a warning," which frames the action as an obligation rather than a personal judgment. He describes this as reinforcing the teacher's image as a trustworthy, consistent leader while explicitly signaling that the consequence doesn't undo the relationship. Based on using the technique hundreds of times, he reports it reliably produces quiet acceptance and even later apologies from students.
points: Difficult students should be held accountable exactly like everyone else — calm, direct, and without added friction.
During the tenuous period when a difficult student is transitioning toward better behavior, one harsh moment can set them back.
A small phrasing adjustment — acknowledging recent improvement before delivering a consequence — protects the relationship without softening accountability.
The key phrase "I have to" reframes the consequence as an obligation rather than a personal judgment against the student.
This approach reinforces the teacher's image as a trustworthy, consistent leader while the consequence still stands.
quotes: How should I hold difficult students accountable? It's a topic I haven't covered specifically because the answer is so simple and direct: Just like everyone else.
It’s a way of enforcing consequences with all students without causing friction or resentment.

Because, when a difficult student is in the midst of transitioning into the well-behaved student you envision them to be, it’s a tenuous time. One stern lecture or burst of anger from you could send them in the opposite direction.
Hey Anthony, I really appreciate how well you’ve been doing, but I have to give you a warning for breaking rule number two.
It reinforces their image of you as a leader to be trusted, as a person of integrity they can count on to do what they say they’re going to do.
The student will look down, nod their head, and say, 'I understand.' You may also receive an apology, although it usually comes at the end of the day.
It’s a simple little change, hard to believe it could make much difference. But for those few students on the cusp of great and enduring change . . . It can mean the world to them.
